Their most recent common ancestor is therefore not a “lion‑zebra” animal but a much older, small, insectivorous mammal that lived in the **Late Cretaceous/Early Paleogene** (about 90–100 million years ago).  

This ancestor is the last common ancestor of the clade **Laurasiatheria**, which includes all of the following orders:

| Order | Common name | Approximate divergence from Laurasiatheria |
|-------|-------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Carnivora | Carnivores (cats, dogs, bears, etc.) | ~90–100 Ma |
| Perissodactyla | Odd‑toed ungulates (horses, rhinos, tapirs) | ~90–100 Ma |
| Artiodactyla | Even‑toed ungulates (deer, cattle, pigs, giraffes) | ~90–100 Ma |
| Chiroptera | Bats | ~90–100 Ma |
| Cetartiodactyla | Whales, dolphins, hippos | ~90–100 Ma |
| Eulipotyphla | Hedgehogs, shrews, moles | ~90–100 Ma |
| Pholidota | Pangolins | ~90–100 Ma |

So, the common ancestor of a lion and a zebra was a small, insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly 90–100 million years ago, before the diversification of the major mammalian lineages that gave rise to modern carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates.
